story.text:
Benjamin Franklin was born in Boston, New England, in a house on Milk Street opposite the Old South Meeting House. [d1ed71b-c0019, d1ed71b-c0800] He was born on Sunday, January 6, old style, 1706. [d1ed71b-c0019, d1ed71b-c0800] Josiah Franklin and Abiah Folger had ten children together, making seventeen children in all from Josiah's two marriages. [d1ed71b-c0275] Benjamin Franklin's family had lived for at least three hundred years at Ecton, Northamptonshire, England, and for many generations the eldest son had been the village blacksmith. [d1ed71b-c0766, d1ed71b-c0274] Benjamin Franklin's father, Josiah Franklin, was an industrious candlemaker in Boston. [d1ed71b-c0765] Josiah Franklin and his wife Abiah lived together for fifty-five years and maintained a large family comfortably by constant labour and honest industry. [d1ed71b-c0855]

Benjamin Franklin was sent to the Boston Grammar-School when he was eight years old but attended for less than a year due to the cost. [d1ed71b-c0765] After leaving the Boston Grammar-School, Franklin went to another school kept by George Brownell where he stayed about a year, ending his formal schooling. [d1ed71b-c0765, d1ed71b-c0766] During his two years of schooling, Franklin learned to read and write but was not very good at arithmetic. [d1ed71b-c0766] Franklin's family was humble but not extremely poor or ignorant, with a long lineage of respectable, plain people. [d1ed71b-c0766] Franklin's father was a strong, active, intelligent, and inquiring man who was respected by his neighbors. [d1ed71b-c0766] Franklin's mother was Abiah Folger, daughter of Peter Folger, a somewhat learned man who taught Indians to read and write and wrote verses. [d1ed71b-c0767] Franklin inherited a fondness for books from his maternal grandfather and family, and at twelve years old he read everything he could find. [d1ed71b-c0767]

After his schooling ended, Franklin entered his father's shop to cut wicks and melt tallow. [d1ed71b-c0766, d1ed71b-c0765] Benjamin Franklin was employed in cutting wick for the candles, filling the dipping mold and the molds for cast candles, attending the shop, and going on errands. [d1ed71b-c0545] Benjamin Franklin had a strong inclination for the sea and ran off when he was sixteen years old. [d1ed71b-c0545]

Benjamin Franklin entered a common-law marriage on September 1, 1730. [d1ed71b-c0510] Deborah Franklin was a good and faithful helpmate who assisted Benjamin Franklin much by attending the shop, and they thrived together. [d1ed71b-c0835] Benjamin Franklin and Deborah Franklin had a friendly companionship, addressing each other affectionately in letters. [d1ed71b-c0835] Benjamin Franklin suffered a pleurisy which very nearly carried him off and had a second attack of this complaint so serious that the left lung suppurated. [d1ed71b-c0305] Benjamin Franklin lived in London in 1726. [d1ed71b-c0583] George III sought to discredit Franklin's scientific opinions by ordering the substitution of blunt for pointed ends on Kew Palace lightning rods. [d1ed71b-c0601] Benjamin Franklin was eminent in science, diplomacy, literature, and public service, inventing the lightning rod and Franklin stove, founding important institutions, and organizing the colonial postal system. [d1ed71b-c0005] Benjamin Franklin was the only statesman who signed the Declaration of Independence, the Treaty of Alliance with France, the Treaty of Peace with England, and the Constitution. [d1ed71b-c0006] Benjamin Franklin had great merit as a philosopher and his discoveries in electricity were very grand. [d1ed71b-c1027] Franklin's discovery of the nature of lightning and invention of the lightning rod earned him widespread popular applause, even if he was not ranked among the greatest scientists. [d1ed71b-c0905] Peter Collinson welcomed Benjamin Franklin and became a lifelong friend who shared enthusiasm for philosophical and human interests. [d1ed71b-c0938] Benjamin Franklin attempted to establish an academy in Philadelphia in 1743 to provide a complete education for youth, reflecting his views on education. [d1ed71b-c0797, d1ed71b-c0358]

Benjamin Franklin died after an abscess in his lungs suddenly burst, causing difficulty in breathing and leading to a calm lethargic state before he quietly expired. [d1ed71b-c0765]

Benjamin Franklin is remembered as a man who achieved wealth, reputation as a diplomatist and statesman, an accomplished scholar, a man of letters of world-wide fame, a philosopher, and an investigator and discoverer in science who enlarged human knowledge. [d1ed71b-c0765] He played a crucial role in securing the independence of the United States and establishing it as a nation, being its ablest champion abroad and contributing to the foreign alliance and funds essential for the American Revolution. [d1ed71b-c0004] Franklin is remembered for his patience, fortitude, practical wisdom, self-sacrificing devotion to his country, and for advancing the material prosperity of his countrymen through his maxims and sayings. [d1ed71b-c0004] He is remembered as a self-made man who rose from humble beginnings by industry, economy, and perseverance in self-improvement to eminence. [d1ed71b-c0004]

SYSTEM:
You check claims about one person. Each claim comes with statements taken from the sources, already rewritten to say exactly who they are about.
For each claim decide whether the statements, read together, state everything the claim says about this person.
- A statement about someone else is not evidence about the person. "Master Thomas's second wife was Rowena Hamilton" does not support "The person's second wife was Rowena Hamilton". A fact about a relative is evidence only when the statement ties that relative to the person ("the person's mother was Harriet").
- Judge facts, not the choice of example. Questions like "the hardest thing" or "a funny story" ask for an example, and sources rarely use those words. If the only unsupported part of a claim is a label like that ("the hardest thing he went through was..."), the verdict is "partial", and "supported_part" is the same fact without the label.
- The claim itself must be about the person, or about someone in relation to the person. A true claim only about someone else ("Colonel Lloyd whipped old Barney") is "unsupported": it is not about the person.
- Paraphrase is fine. Added details (dates, names, places, numbers, causes, feelings, judgments like "leading", "best known", "remembered") are not.
Verdicts:
- "supported": the statements state every part of the claim about this person.
- "partial": they state part of it. Then also give "supported_part": the claim rewritten to say only what the statements state about this person, in one sentence, adding nothing. Empty if nothing useful is left.
- "unsupported": they don't state it, or they are about someone else.
Before the verdict, answer "about_person" for each claim: true only if the claim says something about this person specifically (what they did, what happened to them, who they knew, what they were like). A general statement about a group, a place, an era or slavery in general is false, even if true and even if it affects the person.

You check claims about one person. Each claim comes with statements taken from the sources, already rewritten to say exactly who they are about.
For each claim decide whether the statements, read together, state everything the claim says about this person.

A fact about a relative is evidence only when the statement ties that relative to the person ("the person's mother was Harriet").
- Judge facts, not the choice of example. Questions like "the hardest thing" or "a funny story" ask for an example, and sources rarely use those words. If the only unsupported part of a claim is a label like that ("the hardest thing he went through was..."), the verdict is "partial", and "supported_part" is the same fact without the label.
- The claim itself must be about the person, or about someone in relation to the person. A true claim only about someone else ("Colonel Lloyd whipped old Barney") is "unsupported": it is not about the person.
- Paraphrase is fine. Added details (dates, names, places, numbers, causes, feelings, judgments like "leading", "best known", "remembered") are not.
Verdicts:
- "supported": the statements state every part of the claim about this person.
- "partial": they state part of it. Then also give "supported_part": the claim rewritten to say only what the statements state about this person, in one sentence, adding nothing. Empty if nothing useful is left.
- "unsupported": they don't state it, or they are about someone else.
Before the verdict, answer "about_person" for each claim: true only if the claim says something about this person specifically (what they did, what happened to them, who they knew, what they were like). A general statement about a group, a place, an era or slavery in general is false, even if true and even if it affects the person.

You answer one question using ONLY the source snippets you are given.

- Every claim needs at least one exact quote copied word for word from a snippet (at least 3 words), and the ID of that snippet.
- Never state a date, name, place or number unless it appears in your quote.
- Snippets can be about other people. Only use what they say about the person asked about. Some snippets are written by the person in the first person: there "I" and "my" are the person, while "he", "his" and "her" are usually someone else. Read the sentences around a quote to be sure whose fact it is.
- Say only what the quotes say. Don't add your own summary or judgment ("leading figure", "best known", "remembered as").
- Some questions ask you to pick an example: the hardest time, a funny story, a scary moment, a rival. Picking the passage that best fits is your job, and the sources will rarely use the question's word ("hardest", "funny"). So pick the best fit and state its facts plainly ("Mr. Covey whipped him until his back bled"), without the question's label ("The hardest thing was..."). Only return no claims if no snippet fits at all.
- If the snippets don't answer the question, return no claims.

Write each claim in the third person, in your own words, about the person. Sources written by the person say "I"; your claims say "he" or "she" or the name.
